catalog_quote: Metrical structure as described in §2.3.2 above allows a simple description of word stress: the final foot of the word is prominent. This results in the following pattern: When the final syllable of the word is long, it is stressed. ... When the final syllable of the word is short, the penultimate syllable is stressed.

audit.recode_to: weight (quantity-sensitive, right-edge moraic trochee): primary stress on the final syllable if it has a long vowel (heavy), otherwise on the penult; heavy = (C)Vː only (all VV sequences of unlike vowels are disyllabic and light, loanword codas non-moraic per §2.3.2.1 fn.13); secondary stress on the strong mora of each preceding foot. Drop in the strict set (2-syllable maŋō /maˈŋoː/, matā /maˈtaː/ = 01, not 10). This matches how the catalog already codes the identical Polynesian pattern in Samoan, Tongan, Tuvaluan and Fijian ('weight'). If the catalog wants to keep Gordon-register membership (in the dominant set) it should carry a caution that 'penult' holds only when long vowels are counted as two vowels, an analysis the deciding grammar explicitly rejects.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim in the Kieviet 2017 PDF we hold at §2.4.1 p.45 (record says p.44; one page off). (2) The class 'fixed-strict penult' comes from Gordon 2002's quantity-insensitive appendix (secondary survey, source unprinted; StressTyp2 traces to Du Feu 1996:188), not from the quoted grammar. The quoted grammar -- the best available source, held in full -- says the final syllable is stressed when long (maŋō /maˈŋoː/, keretū /ˌkereˈtuː/, minimal pair ˈmata vs maˈtaː) and analyses long vowels as heavy monosyllables, VV as disyllabic. Under that syllabification the pattern is weight-sensitive, not 'one determinate weight-blind pattern per length'. The earlier domain check even recorded 'weight-conditioned: long final vowel takes stress' but only verified the word domain, so the class was never revisited; the 'verified-clean / no discrepancy' flag is therefore wrong for the class. The catalog codes the same ru

Subsequently, the pitch may gradually drop: [...] The only difference between polar questions and statements is intonational: whereas in statements the final phrase of the sentence is normally pronounced in a low tone, polar questions have a high rise on the final stressed syllable (§2.4.2; cf. Du Feu 1995: 27).
